newsitem.title: JAPAN: HKMA'S YAM SAYS THAI PACKAGE TO CALM ASIA MARKETS.
newsitem.headline: HKMA'S YAM SAYS THAI PACKAGE TO CALM ASIA MARKETS.

text.p: Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) chief executive Joseph Yam said on Monday that Thailand's economic adjustment programme and the international rescue package for the country should restore calm to financial markets in Asia.

"This very credible economic adjustment package and financing package for Thailand should restore calm to financial markets in this region and restore calmness to the currencies of this region," Yam told Reuters Financial Television in an interview.

Asked if the subject is likely to come up at the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) annual meeting in September, Yam said most of the details of the rescue package should have been worked out by then, and the currency turmoil of the past months could be a subject of review at the meeting.
"By the time of the annual IMF meeting, people will, I hope, be in a position to have a post-mortem on what happened in Asia in the last couple months and try and draw lessons from it," he said.
Yam said the Thai economic adjustment package was very credible and this was why participants were willing to pledge $16 billion, exceeding the $14 billion which the IMF saw as the necessary amount.
He said Hong Kong's participation in the rescue package was prompted by what it saw as a need to support Asian monetary cooperation, and in particular, to counter further currency turmoil in Asia.
"(It) was very very important because there was always the danger of a contagion effect affecting economies in this region," he said.
But he added that there was also a greater need for cooperation on all fronts such as the standardisation of monetary standards and the building of financial infrastructure.

He said given the increasing globalisation of financial markets and the rapid pace of financial liberalisation, "there is a need for some sort of solidarity in the Asian region for helping...the maintenance of currency stability in the region."
Asian monetary agreements have developed from a series of bilateral repurchase agreements, aimed at providing liquidity, to support measures including the assumption of credit risk, Yam said.
"I think this is a good way forward," he said.
